items.passage: In an experiment by Matthew Salganik and colleagues, participants downloaded songs by unknown bands from an online market split into eight independent “worlds.” Because participants saw each song’s download count in their own world, a song that topped one world’s rankings could languish in another, suggesting that its success was partly ______ the choices of its earliest listeners.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To be “hostage to” something is to be at its mercy, controlled by things outside one’s own control. Participants saw how often each song had already been downloaded, and the same song could top the rankings in one world and languish in another. Since the songs were identical across worlds, what differed was the earlier downloads, so a song’s success depended in part on the choices of the people who heard it first.

A.why_wrong: If success were “impervious to” early listeners’ choices, it would be unaffected by them, and a song would fare about the same in every world. The text says the same song could top one world’s rankings and languish in another, which shows those choices did affect it.

B.why_wrong: “Antecedent to” means coming before. The earliest listeners chose first, and a song’s success in its world followed from those choices, so the success could not have come before them.

D.why_wrong: “Inimical to” means harmful to. Nothing suggests that a song’s success harmed its earliest listeners’ choices; the relation in the text runs the other way, from early choices to later success.

band7_moves: consequence is the only clue: the reader infers that identical songs diverged because of earlier downloads
familiar word in a transferred sense (hostage to)
all four options past corrected rank 20,000
order-reversal distractor (antecedent to) pairs success with the early choices in the wrong sequence

sources.what: Salganik, Dodds, and Watts (2006, Science): artificial music market with 14,341 participants, eight social-influence worlds where prior downloads were visible; social influence made success more unequal and unpredictable

items.notes: Subject: social science (sociology). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (identical songs diverge across worlds only because of earlier downloads, so success depended on early choices; then match that dependence to the transferred sense of “hostage to”). Concessive frame: no. Transferred-sense key: yes (hostage to fortune). Section 6 checks (corrected ranks): impervious to 20,091; antecedent to 35,359; hostage to 26,698; inimical to 27,949; 4 of 4 past 20,000; mean log 4.43; rarest distractor 35,359. Band-5 guard: clear. Simplified: the study also had an independent condition without download counts.

band7.why: Corrected ranks impervious to 20,091, antecedent to 35,359, hostage to 26,698, inimical to 27,949: 4 of 4 past 20,000, mean log 4.43, rarest distractor 35,359. Two-step consequence inference (identical songs diverge only through earlier downloads) and a familiar word in a transferred sense, as in 3021d9ef and 5e57efec. Hostage is better known than its old-corpus rank says, so the transferred sense carries the key; no distractor survives a loose reading after germane to went.

fixes: trimmed passage to near the models’ median (65 to 58 words)
replaced A immune to (corrected 11,666, a student-familiar word) with impervious to (20,091) so the four options sit in one band
replaced B germane to with antecedent to: read loosely as “related to”, germane to was defensible

items.passage: Records show far more Atlantic tropical storms in recent decades than in the late nineteenth century. Gabriel Vecchi and Thomas Knutson have argued, however, that much of this apparent increase may be ______ changes in observational capabilities: before satellites, a storm that never crossed a shipping lane or approached a coastline could pass entirely unrecorded.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: An “artifact of” something is a result produced by the way it was studied or measured rather than by the thing itself. The colon explains that, before satellites, storms far from ships and coasts went unrecorded, so older records count fewer storms than actually formed. Part of the rise in recorded storms therefore comes from better observation, which makes it an artifact of changes in how storms were observed.

B.why_wrong: An “impediment to” something is an obstacle that hinders it. The text does not present the rise in recorded storms as hindering improvements in observation; it says those improvements produced much of the rise.

C.why_wrong: A “harbinger of” something signals that it is coming. The increase does not foretell changes in observation; according to the text, those changes came first and account for part of the increase.

D.why_wrong: A “vestige of” something is a trace left over from it. The increase is not a remnant of earlier observing methods; it reflects how much more the newer methods detect.

band7_moves: clue is a mechanism after the colon, a level more concrete than the key
key in a transferred sense (artifact of a method)
direction-reversal distractor (impediment to: the increase acting on the changes) set against the passage’s causal order
option set rare throughout; no option echoes the passage

sources.what: Vecchi and Knutson (2008, Journal of Climate) estimate Atlantic tropical storms missed before satellites because of sparse ship tracks; after adjustment the long-term rise in storm counts is weak and not significant

items.notes: Subject: natural science (climate). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (the colon gives a mechanism, missed storms, from which the reader infers that the recorded rise is partly produced by observation; then the key names that relation). Concessive frame: “however” turns against the records. Transferred-sense key: yes (artifact from the laboratory sense). Section 6 checks (corrected ranks): an artifact of 11,666 (modern word, absent from freq.txt); an impediment to 23,789; a harbinger of 32,004; a vestige of 14,248; 4 of 4 past 10,000, 2 past 20,000; mean log 4.28. Band-5 guard: clear. The authors estimate storms missed by the pre-satellite observing network (1878 to 1965).

band7.why: Corrected ranks an artifact of 11,666, an impediment to 23,789, a harbinger of 32,004, a vestige of 14,248: 4 of 4 past 10,000, 2 past 20,000, mean log 4.28. Key in a transferred sense (artifact of a method) inferred from a mechanism after the colon, as in 5a97d9cd; vestige is the near miss (a remnant, not a by-product).

fixes: trimmed passage (61 to 55 words); dropped aircraft reconnaissance, which the source does not discuss
replaced B a justification for (corrected 7,988, under the band) with an impediment to (23,789); same direction-reversal recipe

items.passage: Standard economic models treat money as ______: a household that saves twenty dollars because gasoline has become cheaper should spend that windfall just as it would spend twenty dollars from any other source. Yet when gasoline prices plummeted in 2008, economists Justine Hastings and Jesse Shapiro found, households switched to premium gasoline considerably more frequently than the improvement in their purchasing power could justify.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Money that is “fungible” is interchangeable: any one dollar can stand in for any other. The colon restates this assumption, since the models expect twenty dollars saved on gasoline to be spent exactly like twenty dollars from anywhere else. The finding that households spent their gasoline savings on better gasoline shows them treating those dollars as different, which is why it challenges the assumption.

A.recipe: near synonym that fails on one feature (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: Money is “convertible” when it can be exchanged for another currency or for gold. The colon is about whether dollars from different sources are spent alike, not about exchanging money for something else.

B.why_wrong: “Discretionary” money is money left over to spend as one chooses. The models’ assumption in the colon is that saved dollars are spent like any others, which says nothing about whether the money is optional spending.

C.why_wrong: “Illiquid” money or assets cannot easily be spent or turned into cash. The colon says the models expect the saved twenty dollars to be spent like any other money, the opposite of treating it as hard to spend.

band7_moves: rare key with the restatement after a colon in plain words
every option is an economics term that collocates with money (collocation trap)
near synonym that fails on one feature: convertible (exchange for another form, not interchangeable units)
all four options past rank 20,000

sources.what: Hastings and Shapiro (2013, QJE), Fungibility and Consumer Choice: households shifted toward premium gasoline when gasoline prices fell in 2008 far more than income effects explain, rejecting fungibility of gasoline money

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key letter D. Steps: 1 (colon restatement), carried by vocabulary as section 5 allows for one-step B1 (93665100, bce4d106). Concessive frame: no (Yet introduces the finding). Transferred-sense key: no. Section 6 checks (corrected ranks): fungible and illiquid absent from both corpora (modern finance words, rare for students), convertible 45,653, discretionary 20,866; 4 of 4 past 20,000; rarest distractor unseen. Band-5 guard: clear. Collocation trap: all three distractors are economic adjectives that pair with money. Simplified: the study measured grade shifts with grocery-chain fuel data, 2006 to 2009.

band7.why: Corrected ranks convertible 45,653, discretionary 20,866, illiquid and fungible unseen in both corpora: 4 of 4 past 20,000. One-step colon restatement carried by vocabulary, as 93665100 and bce4d106; every option collocates with money and convertible is the near synonym that fails on one feature. Band-5 guard clear (no distractor under 10,000).

fixes: replaced C nominal (corrected 10,075, the commonest option) with illiquid: read loosely as “at face value” (a dollar is a dollar), nominal came close to the restatement

items.passage: When the United States terminated the bracero program in 1964, barring the Mexican seasonal workers who had done much of its agricultural labor, officials expected the exclusion to prove ______ for American-born farmworkers. Yet economists Michael Clemens and colleagues found that domestic farmworkers’ wages and employment increased no faster in states that had depended heavily on braceros than elsewhere.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Salutary” means beneficial. “Yet” sets the finding against the officials’ expectation, and the finding is that domestic farmworkers’ wages and employment did not increase faster where braceros had been excluded. For that to contradict the expectation, officials must have expected wages and employment to rise, that is, expected the exclusion to benefit American-born farmworkers.

A.why_wrong: “Inconsequential” describes what the economists found, an exclusion with no measurable effect. Officials who had expected no effect would not be contradicted by that finding, but “Yet” marks the finding as a contrast with their expectation.

C.why_wrong: “Deleterious” means harmful. If officials had expected the exclusion to hurt domestic farmworkers, finding that their wages increased no faster where braceros left would not contrast with that expectation.

D.why_wrong: “Precarious” means insecure or risky. The text gives no sign that officials expected the exclusion to make farmworkers’ situation uncertain; the contrast concerns whether wages and employment would rise.

band7_moves: received view then finding, blank on the view being challenged
the finding’s own trait offered as a reversal (inconsequential)
direction of the expectation left implicit, recovered from a negated comparison
all four options past rank 10,000

sources.what: Clemens, Lewis, and Postel: 1964 bracero exclusion was meant to raise domestic farm wages and employment; wages and employment in highly exposed states moved like those in unexposed states; growers adopted labor-saving technology

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (read “Yet” as contrast, then infer the expectation from the negated finding: rose no faster implies an expected rise). Concessive frame: the received view (officials’ expectation) holds the blank and the finding is left implicit about direction. Transferred-sense key: no. Section 6 checks: salutary 23,342; inconsequential 34,175; deleterious 41,092; precarious 13,764; 4 of 4 past 10,000, 3 past 20,000. Band-5 guard: clear. Simplified: the program ended on December 31, 1964; the study notes growers mechanized instead of hiring domestic workers.

band7.why: Corrected ranks inconsequential 34,175, salutary 23,342, deleterious 17,822, precarious 13,764: 4 of 4 past 10,000, 2 past 20,000, mean log 4.32. Received view then finding with the blank on the view (B3, as 22a41819 and e8fb0744); the direction of the expectation is recovered from a negated comparison, and the finding’s own trait (inconsequential) is the reversal.

items.passage:
The following text is from George Gissing’s 1891 novel New Grub Street. Edwin Reardon, an aspiring writer who has exhausted his savings and is approaching starvation, has applied for a clerkship at a London hospital.

The applicant was engaged. He had barely strength to walk home; the sudden relief from his miseries made him, for the first time, <u>sensible</u> of the extreme physical weakness into which he had sunk. For the next week he was very ill, but he did not allow this to interfere with his new work, which was easily learnt and not burdensome.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “sensible” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: Reardon has been hired, and the relief makes him, “for the first time,” notice how weak he has become; the next sentence confirms the weakness by saying he was very ill for a week. To be “sensible of” something in this sense is to be aware of it, so “sensible” most nearly means cognizant.

A.why_wrong: “Sensible” often means showing good judgment, but the sentence is not about Reardon acting wisely; it is about his suddenly noticing his own weakness.

B.why_wrong: In older usage something “sensible” can be perceptible, able to be noticed by the senses. Here the word describes Reardon, who notices the weakness, not something that can be noticed.

D.why_wrong: Being disdainful of something means scorning it. The text gives no sign that Reardon looks down on his weakness; the relief simply makes him aware of it for the first time.

band7_moves: common target in a non-first sense (sensible of = aware of)
key mid-frequency (Cognizant), not the plain everyday synonym
two distractors are real senses of the target (judicious, perceptible)
near miss on one feature: disdainful (an attitude toward the weakness, not awareness of it)

sources.what: Text of New Grub Street (1891), chapter V, copied from Project Gutenberg

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter C. Excerpt copied exactly (one paragraph, chapter V). Steps: 2 (set aside the everyday sense, then read the frame “sensible of” with the clue that he notices his weakness for the first time). Transferred-sense key: yes (archaic sense, aware). Rare clue: no. Option ranks (corrected): Judicious 12,231; Perceptible 7,266; Cognizant 28,383; Disdainful 14,656; mean log 4.14. Key mid-frequency rather than the plain synonym “Aware,” as section 5 asks for M1. Two real senses of the target plus one near miss.

band7.why: Corrected ranks Judicious 12,231, Perceptible 7,266, Cognizant 28,383, Disdainful 14,656: mean log 4.14, above both CB M1 band-7 items (6557f7fc 3.88, 7f935017 3.84). Archaic sense (sensible of) held against two real senses, one of them the everyday meaning; mid-rare key. Weaker than the Wharton model in one respect: Judicious and Perceptible fail on the “of” frame rather than fitting loosely.

fixes: replaced D Suspicious (3,985) with Disdainful (14,656): Suspicious sat far below the other options and, with Perceptible, tripped the band-5 guard (key rarest, two distractors under 10,000)

items.passage: Researchers Frances Trix and Carolyn Psenka analyzed more than 300 recommendation letters for candidates for faculty positions at an American medical school and found that letters for women were more often ______ than letters for men. Such letters tended to be brief and to offer only generalized praise, saying little about the candidate’s research or other particular accomplishments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A “perfunctory” letter is one written with the minimum of effort, as a routine obligation. The second sentence describes exactly such letters: brief, offering only generalized praise, and saying little about the candidate’s particular work. Those features are what make a recommendation letter perfunctory.

B.why_wrong: An “effusive” letter gushes with praise. The text says the letters offered only general praise and said little, the opposite of an effusive letter.

C.why_wrong: A “prolix” letter is long-winded. The text says these letters tended to be brief.

D.why_wrong: An “uncomplimentary” letter is critical of its subject. The letters described do offer praise, though only in general terms; the text faults them for saying little, not for criticizing the applicant.

band7_moves: key is the abstract category the described features instantiate
two reversals on different features (effusive: amount of praise; prolix: length)
near miss on one feature: uncomplimentary (negative tone, but the letters do praise)
all four options past rank 10,000

sources.what: Trix and Psenka (2003, Discourse & Society 14(2)), Exploring the Color of Glass: over 300 letters of recommendation for medical faculty at a large American medical school; letters for women shorter and more often lacking specifics

items.notes: Subject: social science (sociolinguistics). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (generalize from the described features, short, general praise, few specifics, to the abstract category). Concessive frame: no. Transferred-sense key: no. Section 6 checks: perfunctory 14,278; effusive 19,725; prolix 47,476; uncomplimentary 33,455; 4 of 4 past 10,000, 2 past 20,000; rarest distractor 47,476 (just under 50,000). Band-5 guard: clear. Trix and Psenka call these “letters of minimal assurance.” Psenka’s role is not stated because it was not checked.

band7.why: Corrected ranks perfunctory 14,278, effusive 19,725, prolix 47,476, uncomplimentary 33,455: 4 of 4 past 10,000, 2 past 20,000, mean log 4.41. Abstract category pinned by the described features (B4, as a06c434d); two reversals on different features and a near miss on tone (uncomplimentary: the letters do praise).

fixes: trimmed passage (63 to 58 words)

items.passage: Museum visitors may imagine that they contemplate celebrated paintings at length, but their viewing is seldom ______. Observing visitors in the galleries of the Metropolitan Museum, researchers Jeffrey Smith and Lisa Smith found that people spent a median of approximately 17 seconds examining each of six renowned masterpieces.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Leisurely” means unhurried. The text contrasts what visitors imagine, contemplating paintings at length, with what the researchers observed: a median of about 17 seconds per work. Viewing that brief is seldom leisurely.

A.why_wrong: Whether visitors look alone or with others is not the point of the contrast, which concerns how long they look.

B.why_wrong: “Cursory” means hasty. A median of 17 seconds is cursory viewing, so saying it is seldom cursory contradicts the finding.

C.why_wrong: “Orderly” describes viewing that follows a neat, systematic sequence. The finding concerns the length of time visitors spend, not whether they look in an orderly way.

sources.what: Smith and Smith (2001), Spending time on art: 150 visitors at the Metropolitan Museum of Art viewing six works; mean 27.2 seconds, median 17.0 seconds

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology of art). Key letter D. Negation in “seldom.” The six works are not named in the passage because they were not checked.

fixes: trimmed passage (52 to 48 words)

items.passage: Artist Lalla Essaydi’s photographic series Les Femmes du Maroc is ______ nineteenth-century European paintings of harem women. Essaydi restages works such as Ingres’s La Grande Odalisque but covers her models in Arabic calligraphy written in henna, countering the painters’ fantasies of silent, exotic women with images of women wrapped in writing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A “rejoinder to” something is a reply to it, often one that answers back. Essaydi restages the European paintings, but she changes them in order to counter the painters’ fantasies, so her series answers those paintings rather than simply copying them.

A.why_wrong: Essaydi does restage the paintings, but the text stresses that she alters them to counter the painters’ fantasies; “an imitation of” captures only the restaging.

C.why_wrong: The paintings are from the nineteenth century and Essaydi’s series came later, so her work could not have inspired them; the influence runs the other way.

D.why_wrong: A supplement adds to something in the same spirit. Essaydi’s series counters the paintings’ view of women rather than extending it.

sources.what: Lalla Essaydi, Les Femmes du Maroc: restages Orientalist paintings by Ingres, Delacroix, and Gerome; women and surfaces covered in henna calligraphy
Les Femmes du Maroc: La Grande Odalisque (2008), a response to Ingres’s Grande Odalisque with henna calligraphy (VMFA)

items.notes: Subject: humanities and arts (photography). Key letter B. Titles are italic in print. “Countering the painters’ fantasies” is the passage’s evaluative clue; the key does not repeat it.

fixes: trimmed passage (56 to 51 words); "paintings of North African women" made "paintings of harem women" since La Grande Odalisque is not a North African scene

items.passage: Philadelphia ceramicist Roberto Lugo ______ two traditions that seldom intersect. He produces porcelain vases and teapots in ornate shapes long associated with European royalty, then decorates them with graffiti-inspired patterns and portraits, often pairing a historical figure such as Frederick Douglass with a rapper such as Notorious B.I.G. on a single vessel.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The second sentence explains what Lugo does with the two traditions: the ornate shapes come from porcelain long associated with European royalty, and the decoration comes from graffiti and from portraits that pair historical figures with rappers, all on a single vessel. Bringing the two together in one work is to integrate them.

B.why_wrong: Combining hip-hop portraits with ornate porcelain might seem playful, but nothing in the text says Lugo mocks either tradition; it describes him uniting them.

C.why_wrong: To “sunder” is to split apart. Lugo brings the traditions together on the same vessel.

D.why_wrong: To catalog is to list or classify. Lugo makes new objects that combine the traditions; he is not recording them.

sources.what: Roberto Lugo works in centuries-old European and Asian porcelain traditions associated with royalty, mixing in hip-hop and graffiti; often pairs Black or Latino historical figures (Frederick Douglass among them) with rappers such as Notorious B.I.G.

items.notes: Subject: humanities and arts (ceramics). Key letter A. Restatement in the next sentence.

fixes: trimmed passage (55 to 52 words); "eighteenth-century European luxury wares" replaced by shapes long associated with European royalty and the pairing stated as the source gives it (historical figures with rappers)
explanation or why_wrong updated to the trimmed passage

items.passage: When Mary Ann Shadd founded the Provincial Freeman, an antislavery newspaper for Black communities in Canada, in 1853, she placed the name of abolitionist Samuel Ringgold Ward, rather than her own, on its masthead as editor. Knowing that many readers regarded newspaper work as a man’s profession, Shadd evidently hoped to ______ objections to a woman directing the publication.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “forestall” something is to prevent it by acting in advance. Shadd knew many readers regarded newspaper work as a man’s profession, so she kept her own name off the masthead and listed a man instead; that step was meant to keep objections to a woman editor from arising in the first place.

A.why_wrong: Listing a man as editor would avoid objections, not stir them up, so “provoke” reverses Shadd’s purpose.

B.why_wrong: To rebut objections is to answer them with arguments after they are made. Shadd did not argue against objections; she hid her role so that they would not arise.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests Shadd wanted to record objections; her action was aimed at avoiding them.

sources.what: Shadd founded the Provincial Freeman (1853) and asked Samuel Ringgold Ward to lend his name as editor; she knew her name on the masthead could alienate readers who considered editorships men's affairs
Shadd feared a woman’s name on the masthead would drive away readers; Ward listed as editor (Canadian Encyclopedia)

items.notes: Subject: history. Key letter C. Cause clue: “Knowing that many readers regarded newspaper work as a man’s profession.”

fixes: added a reachable source for the core claim (biographi.ca did not resolve here); passage unchanged

items.passage:
The following text is from Herbert Quick’s 1922 novel Vandemark’s Folly. The narrator recalls the settlement of his township in Iowa.

Buckner Gowdy, Doctor Bliven, their associates, and others not yet mentioned will be found helping to make or mar the story all through the future; for an Iowa community was like a growing child in this, that its character in maturity was <u>fixed</u> by its beginnings.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “fixed” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The narrator compares an Iowa community to a growing child: what it becomes as an adult depends on its early years. A character “fixed by its beginnings” is one settled or determined by them, which is why the people present at the start will shape the whole story.

A.why_wrong: To fix something can mean to repair it, but a community’s character is not being mended by its beginnings.

B.why_wrong: To fix something can mean to fasten it in place, but the sentence is about what shapes the community’s character, not about attaching anything.

C.why_wrong: To fix a contest can mean to rig or manipulate it, but nothing in the sentence suggests anyone dishonestly controlling the community; the point is that its early years settle its character.

sources.what: Text of Vandemark's Folly (1922), copied from Project Gutenberg

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter D. Excerpt copied exactly (one paragraph). Abstract sense of a common word, as in the medium models (assumed, quality).

fixes: shortened the intro (73 to 67 words); excerpt unchanged

items.passage: Quilter Rosie Lee Tompkins rarely followed a predetermined pattern. Instead, she ______ her designs as she worked, assembling scraps of fabric in vibrant colors and irregular shapes into quilts that often resemble abstract paintings more than traditional bedcovers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The first sentence says Tompkins rarely followed a predetermined pattern, and “Instead” introduces what she did: worked out her designs while making the quilts, with irregular shapes. Making something up as one goes is improvising.

A.why_wrong: Copying a design would mean following an existing pattern, which the text says Tompkins rarely did.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Tompkins bought her designs; the text says she worked them out as she sewed.

D.why_wrong: The text describes Tompkins completing quilts in vibrant colors and irregular shapes, not giving designs up.

sources.what: Rosie Lee Tompkins: improvisational patchwork that sometimes cites familiar quilt patterns but never adheres to them (LRB on the BAMPFA retrospective)

items.notes: Subject: humanities and arts (quilting). Key letter B. Restatement clue: “rarely followed a predetermined pattern.”

fixes: trimmed passage (40 to 38 words)

items.passage: Land birds are a surprisingly ______ component of the diet of tiger sharks in the northern Gulf of Mexico. Marcus Drymon and colleagues discovered the remains of such birds in the stomachs of 41 of the 105 sharks they examined.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: The second sentence gives the evidence: 41 of the 105 sharks examined had eaten land birds. Since more than a third of the sharks had eaten them, land birds are a frequent part of these sharks’ diet.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about land birds being dangerous for sharks to eat.

B.why_wrong: Finding land birds in 41 of 105 sharks shows that such meals are common, not rare.

C.why_wrong: The text reports only how often land birds turn up in the sharks’ stomachs; it does not say the sharks seek the birds out on purpose.

sources.what: Drymon et al. (2019, Ecology), Tiger sharks eat songbirds: 41 of 105 tiger sharks sampled in the north-central Gulf of Mexico had eaten land birds of 11 species; most in fall migration

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine biology). Key letter D. Clue: 41 of 105 sharks.

fixes: trimmed passage (57 to 40 words); "juvenile" and "songbirds" dropped (the source counts 105 tiger sharks of all ages and land birds of 11 species, not all songbirds); brown thrasher detail cut
explanation or why_wrong updated to the trimmed passage

items.passage: Pardhan Gond artist Jangarh Singh Shyam grew up decorating the walls of village houses in central India. After painter Jagdish Swaminathan brought him to Bhopal in the 1980s, Shyam ______ this tradition to paper and canvas, producing vibrant depictions of animals and deities.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Shyam had painted on village walls, and in Bhopal he began working on paper and canvas. Changing a wall-painting tradition so that it suits new surfaces is adapting it.

B.why_wrong: The text describes Shyam making new paintings on paper and canvas, not explaining the tradition to anyone.

C.why_wrong: Nothing suggests Shyam set the tradition beside paper and canvas to compare them; he carried it onto those surfaces.

D.why_wrong: To return something is to bring it back. The tradition had been practiced on mud walls, so moving it to paper and canvas was not a return.

sources.what: Jangarh Singh Shyam: J. Swaminathan found him painting on house walls in the 1980s and brought him to Bhopal (Roopankar, Bharat Bhavan), where he moved his work from walls to paper and canvas

items.notes: Subject: humanities and arts (Gond painting). Key letter A. Easy-tier distractor mix: three unsupported words.

fixes: trimmed passage (52 to 43 words); "early 1980s" made "1980s" as the source gives it

items.passage:
The following text is from W. H. Hudson’s 1918 memoir Far Away and Long Ago, which recalls his childhood in Argentina.

In spring and early summer the low-lying areas about Canada Seca were pleasant places to see and ride on where the pigs had not defaced them: they <u>kept</u> their bright verdure when the higher grounds were parched and brown; then too, after rain, they were made beautiful with the bright little yellow flower called macachina.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “kept” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The low-lying areas stayed bright green while the higher ground dried out and turned brown. They “kept” their verdure, or greenness, in the sense that they retained it.

A.why_wrong: People can keep a holiday by celebrating it, but the low grounds are not celebrating their greenness; they still have it while other land dries out.

items.passage: Retail chains in the United States could increase profits by varying prices across neighborhoods, yet Stefano DellaVigna and Matthew Gentzkow found that most chains’ prices are largely ______ local conditions: a chain’s stores charge nearly identical prices regardless of whether their customers are wealthy or poor and whether competition is intense or weak.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Unresponsive to” means not changing in reaction to. The text says that a chain’s stores charge nearly the same prices whatever the income of their customers and however much competition they face, even though the chains could earn more by varying them. The prices, in other words, do not change with local conditions.

A.why_wrong: Prices “calibrated to” local conditions would be adjusted to fit each neighborhood, so they would differ from store to store. The text says the stores charge nearly the same prices.

B.why_wrong: “Inflated by” means pushed up by. The text never says that local conditions raise a chain’s prices; it says prices stay nearly the same whether customers are wealthy or poor.

D.why_wrong: Prices “tethered to” local conditions would be tied to them and so would move with them, which is the opposite of what DellaVigna and Gentzkow found.

sources.what: DellaVigna and Gentzkow, Uniform Pricing in US Retail Chains (NBER w23996; QJE 2019): most US food, drugstore and mass-merchandise chains charge nearly uniform prices across stores despite wide variation in consumer demographics and competition; the median chain sacrifices about $16m of annual profit; uniform pricing raises the prices poorer households pay relative to the rich

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (nearly the same prices whatever the customers or competition, although varying them would pay, so prices do not change with local conditions). Two reversals that tie prices to local conditions in different ways (fitted to, tied to) and one unsupported direction (pushed up by). Simplified: the paper also estimates the profit forgone and covers several kinds of chains; only the core finding is used. Raw freq.txt ranks: calibrated to 49,423; inflated by 22,778; unresponsive to 21,484; tethered to 17,743.

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target. Corrected option ranks 8,400 to 22,800 (3 of 4 past 10,000, mean log 4.22), one band; two steps (a concessive “could increase profits ... yet” plus a restating colon). Two reversals (calibrated to, tethered to) fall to the same stated fact, so not band 7.

items.passage: Much of composer Éliane Radigue’s electronic music evolves at a ______ pace, unfolding through a series of almost imperceptible tonal shifts: each of the three compositions in her Adnos cycle, which she created on an ARP 2500 synthesizer over eight years in the 1970s and 1980s, transforms over approximately 70 minutes.

items.explanation: “Glacial” here means extremely slow. The text says that Radigue’s music moves through tonal shifts so small they are almost imperceptible and that each Adnos piece takes roughly 70 minutes to transform, so the music changes very slowly.

B.why_wrong: “Frenetic” means wildly fast and excited. Shifts that are almost imperceptible and pieces that transform over 70 minutes describe music that changes slowly, not frantically.

C.why_wrong: “Staccato” is a musical term for short, sharply separated notes. The text describes the music as unfolding through tiny shifts, which suggests smooth, gradual change rather than abrupt, detached sounds.

D.why_wrong: “Erratic” means irregular and unpredictable. The text says nothing about sudden or irregular changes; it stresses how small and gradual the shifts are.

items.passage: Because subtle biases can operate without conscious awareness, one might expect them to be ______, persisting even once identified. Yet Devin Pope, Joseph Price, and Justin Wolfers found that after a study showing that NBA referees called more fouls against players of a different race attracted widespread media attention in 2007, the referees’ bias disappeared.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Intractable” means hard to change or get rid of. The blank describes what one might expect of biases that operate without conscious awareness: that they would persist even after being identified. “Yet” then introduces the contrasting finding that the referees’ bias disappeared once it was publicized.

A.recipe: reversal: trait of the wrong side (ANT)
A.why_wrong: “Ephemeral” means short-lived. That describes what the researchers actually found, since the bias disappeared, not the expectation the blank describes, which “Yet” sets against the finding.

B.why_wrong: “Idiosyncratic” means peculiar to an individual. Nothing in the text concerns biases differing from person to person, and the word does not fit the restatement “persisting even once identified.”

C.why_wrong: “Willful” means deliberate and intentional. The text says these biases can operate without people’s awareness, so one would not expect them to be intentional.

sources.what: Pope, Price and Wolfers, Awareness Reduces Racial Bias (NBER w19765; Management Science 2018): bias in NBA referees’ foul calls persisted until widespread media attention in May 2007 following an academic study, then completely disappeared

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (the expectation is set up by a reason and a restatement, and “Yet” contrasts it with the finding; the finding’s own trait, ephemeral, is the trap). The expectation is framed as a reasoned guess (“one might expect”), not attributed to anyone. Simplified: the 2007 study was Price and Wolfers’s own; the bias was against players of the opposite race from the refereeing crew. Raw freq.txt ranks: ephemeral 21,660; idiosyncratic unseen; willful 21,615; intractable 38,422.

band7.why: Meets its band-6 target. All four options past 20,000 (mean log 4.81) and the band-7 B3 shape (blank on the expectation, the finding’s trait ephemeral as the trap), but the appositive “persisting even once identified” glosses the key, so it is one step for a student who knows intractable.

items.passage: In colonial India, agriculture depended on rainfall, and regional famines were commonplace. But as railroads reached more and more districts between 1861 and 1930, economists Robin Burgess and Dave Donaldson found, a rainfall shortfall in a district became less ______: local prices and mortality rates grew less responsive to it.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Calamitous” means disastrous. Burgess and Donaldson found that once railroads reached a district, local prices and mortality rates responded less to a shortfall of rain. A drought that no longer drove up prices and deaths as much was less of a disaster for the people there.

A.recipe: wrong nuance: frequency instead of severity (CONNOT)
A.why_wrong: “Recurrent” means happening again and again. Railroads could not change how often rain fell short; the text says only that prices and mortality rates responded less to a shortfall, which concerns how harmful it was, not how often it happened.

C.why_wrong: “Acrimonious” means bitter and angry, as a quarrel can be. The text says nothing about disputes over rainfall shortfalls.

D.why_wrong: “Quotidian” means ordinary or everyday. The text says nothing about shortfalls becoming more or less ordinary; it describes how much they affected prices and mortality rates.

band7_moves: negation hidden in a comparative (“became less ______”), as in d7807ec8 (“less ______ observers countered”)
near-synonym distractor that fails on one feature: recurrent (how often) against calamitous (how harmful)
all four options past rank 20,000; rarest distractor unseen in freq.txt
clue in the economists’ register (prices and death rates less responsive) one level more abstract than the key

sources.what: Burgess and Donaldson, Can Openness to Trade Reduce Income Volatility? Evidence from Colonial India’s Famine Era (LSE 2012): railroads expanding 1861 to 1930, rain-fed agriculture and commonplace regional famines; railroads made local prices less responsive to rainfall shocks, and mortality rates became significantly less responsive to rainfall shocks

items.notes: Subject: social science (economic history). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (prices and death rates less responsive to a shortfall, so a shortfall did less harm; reject the frequency reading). No negation-flip distractor (the band-7 B5 recipe). Simplified: the paper also reports real incomes becoming less responsive; only prices and mortality are used. Raw freq.txt ranks: recurrent 23,668; calamitous 40,225; acrimonious 43,432; quotidian unseen.

band7.why: All four options past corrected 20,000 (calamitous 40,225; rarest distractor quotidian unseen; mean log 4.90), key not the rarest (band-5 guard clear). Negation hidden in the comparative “less ______” (band-7 B5 recipe, as d7807ec8), two steps (less responsive prices and deaths, so less harm), and recurrent and quotidian are built from the earlier “famines were commonplace” (frequency, not severity), as inconspicuousness is in 6017ae31. None fits: railroads cannot change how often rain fails.

items.passage:
The following text is from Harold Frederic’s 1896 novel The Damnation of Theron Ware. Theron has abruptly informed his wife, Alice, that he must depart tonight.

Alice’s face showed surprise, but no trace of suspicion. She spoke with <u>studied</u> amiability during the meal, and deferred with such unexpected tact to his implied desire not to be questioned as to the mysterious motives of the journey, that his mood instinctively softened and warmed toward her, as they finished supper.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “studied” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: As used here, “studied” describes Alice’s amiability as something she produces on purpose. She is surprised by Theron’s sudden journey yet shows no suspicion, and she defers “with such unexpected tact” to his wish not to be questioned: her friendliness is a careful, intentional effort, so “studied” most nearly means deliberate.

A.why_wrong: To study something can mean to scrutinize it, or examine it closely, but Alice is not examining anything; “studied” describes the kind of amiability she shows.

B.why_wrong: A studied person can be learned, or scholarly, but nothing in the text concerns learning; the word describes the care Alice takes in being friendly.

D.why_wrong: The text says Alice’s face showed “no trace of suspicion,” so her amiability is not distrustful; she defers to Theron with “unexpected tact,” and his mood warms toward her.

sources.what: Text of The Damnation of Theron Ware (Harold Frederic, 1896), copied from Project Gutenberg

items.notes: Subject: literature. Key letter C. Excerpt copied exactly (one paragraph); the intro summarizes Theron’s speech just before it (“I find I must go to Albany tonight”). Target studied is an everyday word in its adjectival sense (done with deliberate effort). Steps: 2 (set aside the everyday sense; read the surprise and the unexpected tact as signs of effort). Written as band 6: the M1 band-6 model 9b22bf7b keys Dictate against senses of determine. Raw freq.txt ranks: Scrutinized 18,297; Scholarly 5,349; Deliberate 4,546; Distrustful 23,256. Reviewer: hardened from Examined, Academic, Reluctant (mean log rank 3.57, under the band-6 M1 model 9b22bf7b at 3.67 and the band-7 M1 models at 3.84 to 3.88; two distractors made no sense in the sentence and Reluctant could be read loosely as “forced”). Now two rarer senses of study (scrutinize, learned) and a topic echo of “suspicion” that the text rules out; all four options between ranks 4,500 and 23,000, mean log 4.00. Senses that would be a second answer (premeditated, calculated, contrived, affected, feigned, rehearsed) kept out.

band7.why: Was nearer band 5: two distractors (Examined, Academic) made no sense in the sentence and the set sat at mean log 3.57. After the fix all four options sit at 4,500 to 23,000 (mean log 4.00, above the band-6 and band-7 M1 models), the target is a secondary sense of an everyday word, and two distractors are real senses of study. No band-7 claim: M1 band 7 relies on senses that fit loosely, which this item avoids by design.

fixes: hardened: options Examined, Academic, Reluctant replaced by Scrutinized, Scholarly, Distrustful (mean log rank 3.57 to 4.00, one frequency band; Reluctant could be read loosely as forced); why_wrong rewritten

items.passage: A snowshoe hare whose coat has turned white for winter is hardly ______ on brown, snowless ground. B.why_wrong: Saying the hare is “hardly vulnerable” would mean it is safe, but the text says mismatched hares were noticeable to predators and had lower weekly survival.

C.why_wrong: “Nocturnal” means active at night. The text is about whether a hare’s coat matches the ground, not about when hares are active.

D.why_wrong: “Sluggish” means slow-moving. The text says nothing about how fast the hares move; it is about how visible they are.

items.passage: The bioluminescence of New Zealand glowworm larvae (Arachnocampa luminosa) is ______ their feeding strategy. Each larva constructs a silk nest on a cave ceiling and suspends as many as 30 silk threads studded with adhesive droplets; its light then attracts small flying insects, particularly midges, into those sticky filaments.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Integral to” means essential to. The text explains that a glowworm larva catches food with sticky threads and that its light is what draws flies into them, so the glow is an essential part of how the larvae feed.

A.why_wrong: “Incidental to” means a minor side feature of. The light is what draws prey into the threads, so it is central to feeding, not incidental.

B.why_wrong: “Detrimental to” means harmful to. The glow helps the larvae feed by luring flies into their threads; nothing suggests it hinders feeding.

C.why_wrong: “Reminiscent of” means calling to mind. The glow is part of the larvae’s way of feeding, not something that brings it to mind.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Arachnocampa luminosa: endemic to New Zealand; the larva spins a silk nest on the cave ceiling and hangs down up to 30 silk threads with small sticky droplets; the glow acts as bait, attracting prey (largely small Diptera, especially midges) into the threads

items.passage: Analyzing vocabulary from 2,474 languages, Joshua Conrad Jackson and colleagues found that all language families categorize emotions primarily by how pleasant and how physiologically arousing they are, yet emotion concepts are also ______ cultures: Nakh-Dagestanian languages associate “grief” with “fear” and “anxiety,” whereas Tai-Kadai languages associate it with “regret.”
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Divergent across” means differing from one to another. After noting what all language families share, the text turns with “yet” to differences: grief is linked with fear and anxiety in one family of languages but with regret in another. Emotion concepts therefore differ across cultures.

A.why_wrong: If emotion concepts were indistinguishable across cultures, “grief” would be grouped with the same emotions everywhere, but the text gives an example in which it is not.

C.why_wrong: Concepts “insulated from” culture would be shielded from its influence. The example shows the meaning of “grief” differing between language families, so these concepts are not shielded from cultural differences.

D.why_wrong: “Subordinate to” means ranked below. The text does not compare the importance of emotion concepts and cultures; it shows that the concepts differ from one group of languages to another.

items.passage: On September 8, 1965, Larry Itliong and more than 1,000 Filipino farmworkers walked off vineyards in Delano, California. items.passage: Carmen Sanchez and David Dunning found that a little learning can make people’s confidence ______ their competence. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Disproportionate to” means out of proportion with, here too large for. The participants were not overconfident at first, but after a few practice cases their confidence surged, while their performance improved only gradually. Confidence had therefore outrun ability: it became greater than their competence justified.

A.why_wrong: Confidence “commensurate with” competence would match it. The text says the participants’ confidence surged after a few cases while their performance improved only gradually, so the two did not match.

B.why_wrong: “Conducive to” means helping to bring about. The text never says that the participants’ confidence improved their performance; it describes confidence rising much faster than performance.

D.why_wrong: Confidence “subordinate to” competence would be lesser than or ruled by it. The text says the participants became more confident than their performance warranted, the opposite relation.

items.passage: Among deep-sea hydrothermal vents, those of the Lost City field in the Atlantic Ocean are strikingly ______. B.why_wrong: Vents that are “extinct” no longer vent at all. The text says that venting at Lost City is powered by heat from chemical alterations of the rock, so the vents are active, not at rest.

items.passage: When composer Julius Eastman was evicted from his apartment in the 1980s, the scores he kept there were discarded. That loss nonetheless failed to render his compositions ______: because the pieces had been performed, musicians have subsequently been able to reconstruct some of the scores from archival recordings.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Irretrievable” means impossible to recover. Losing his scores might seem to mean losing the music itself, but the text explains why it did not: the pieces had been performed, so musicians have been able to rebuild some of the scores from archival recordings. The loss did not make the compositions impossible to recover.

A.why_wrong: “Ostentatious” means showy. The text is about whether Eastman’s music survived the loss of his scores, and the reason it gives, that recordings let musicians reconstruct the scores, has nothing to do with showiness.

C.why_wrong: “Saccharine” means overly sweet or sentimental. Losing the scores would not make music sentimental, and the recordings the text mentions explain only how the music was recovered.

D.why_wrong: “Derivative” means imitating the work of others. Losing his scores could not make Eastman’s music unoriginal, and the text says nothing about whether it borrows from other composers; it is about whether the music could be recovered.

items.passage: The skin of African spiny mice tears under such low tension that a predator’s grip on these rodents is ______: a captured mouse can escape by shedding a patch of skin. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Precarious” means insecure or likely to give way. Because the mice’s skin tears so easily, a predator holding one may be left with only a patch of skin while the mouse escapes. The predator’s hold, in other words, cannot be relied on.

B.why_wrong: “Inexorable” means impossible to stop or resist. The text says the opposite: the skin tears so easily that a captured mouse can escape by shedding a patch of it.

C.why_wrong: “Rapacious” means greedy and is often said of predators, but the text is not about the predator’s appetite; it is about whether its grip can hold a mouse whose skin tears easily.

D.why_wrong: “Prehensile” means adapted for grasping, as a monkey’s tail is. The text is not about whether a predator’s body is built to grasp prey; it says the mouse’s skin tears so easily that the predator’s hold gives way.

items.passage: Conventional wisdom holds that waiting is ______ customer satisfaction, so faster service should always please customers more. Yet in experiments simulating online travel searches, Ryan Buell and Michael Norton found that people preferred a site that made them wait while showing the work it was doing over one returning identical results instantly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “A drain on” means something that steadily uses up or reduces. The text says that, according to conventional wisdom, faster service should always please customers more, which follows only if waiting reduces satisfaction. The word “Yet” then sets Buell and Norton’s finding, that people sometimes preferred to wait, against that conventional view.

A.recipe: reversal (ANT), trait of the finding rather than of the view
A.why_wrong: If waiting were a spur to satisfaction, slower service would please customers more, the opposite of the conventional view that faster service is always better. A spur to satisfaction is closer to what Buell and Norton found, but the blank describes the view their finding is set against.

C.why_wrong: Calling waiting a barometer of satisfaction would make it only a measure or sign of satisfaction. That would not explain why faster service should always please customers more; the conventional view is that waiting actively lowers satisfaction.

D.why_wrong: If waiting were unrelated to satisfaction, the speed of a service would not matter to customers, so there would be no reason to think faster service should always please them more.

sources.what: Buell and Norton 2011, The Labor Illusion: How Operational Transparency Increases Perceived Value (Management Science): conventional wisdom and operations theory hold that the longer people wait, the less satisfied they become; when websites signal that they are working, people can prefer slower sites to instant ones even when results are identical; five experiments simulated online travel and online dating services

items.notes: Subject: social science (operations, consumer behavior). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (the “so” clause says faster service should always please more, so waiting must reduce satisfaction; “Yet” marks the finding as against this view, which keeps the finding’s trait, a spur, out of the blank). Distractors: one reversal that describes the finding rather than the conventional view (a spur to), one near miss of relation (a barometer of), one reversal (unrelated to). Raw freq.txt ranks: a spur to 6,779; a drain on 9,534; a barometer of 17,917; unrelated to 40,068. items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Impermanent” means not lasting. The text contrasts Tanabe’s craft works, which are made to endure, with his installations, and then explains that each installation is taken apart after its exhibition, its bamboo reused, so that only viewers’ impressions of it remain. The installations are therefore impermanent by design.

A.recipe: reversal (ANT), trait of the other side
A.why_wrong: Durability belongs to Tanabe’s craft works, which the text says are made to endure. The installations are contrasted with them and are dismantled after each exhibition, so they are not durable.

B.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the installations serving a practical purpose; it describes only how long they last, being taken apart after each exhibition.

D.why_wrong: “Monumental” suggests something imposing and lasting, like a monument. The text says nothing about the installations’ size and stresses instead that each one is dismantled after its exhibition, leaving only an impression.

sources.what: Seiko Presage museum interview with fourth-generation bamboo artist Tanabe Chikuunsai IV: after each exhibition the studio carefully dismantles the installation and reuses about 95% of the bamboo strips in future works; craft works are made to endure; of an installation, what remains is the impression it has made on people

items.notes: Subject: humanities (sculpture, craft). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (contrast with craft works made to endure, then the dismantling and reuse after each exhibition; the reader must turn both into a statement about duration). Ephemeral avoided: it is an existing option. Distractors: the other side’s trait (durable), one unsupported (utilitarian), one wrong-connotation word that also implies permanence (monumental). Raw freq.txt ranks: durable 30,496; utilitarian 31,827; impermanent absent (modern word); monumental 23,472. Transient avoided: w2b7_06 offers transitory.

Options one band (raw 23,472 to 31,827; impermanent unseen in freq.txt but built on permanent); band-5 guard passes (one distractor under 10,000 corrected). Easy end of band 6; dropping made to endure would let monumental (large scale) fit the first sentence, so not hardened that way.

items.passage: Parrots and crows rival primates on complex cognitive tasks despite their smaller brains, which seemed to imply that birds make efficient use of ______ neural resources. But Seweryn Olkowicz and colleagues discovered that parrots and songbirds pack neurons so densely that a macaw’s forebrain holds more neurons than a macaque monkey’s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Meager” means small in amount. The text says that birds’ smaller brains seemed to imply something about their neural resources, and the word “But” introduces a finding that contradicts it: parrots and songbirds pack in so many neurons that a macaw’s forebrain has more than a macaque’s. The implied view, then, was that birds have only meager neural resources.

B.why_wrong: Copious neural resources are what Olkowicz and colleagues found. The blank, however, states what small brains seemed to imply, and “But” sets the finding against that implication, so the implication cannot already be that the resources are copious.

C.why_wrong: Small brains might suggest that birds’ neurons work differently, but the finding introduced by “But” concerns how many neurons birds have. Only a claim about amount is contradicted by learning that a macaw’s forebrain holds more neurons than a macaque’s.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that small brains implied supplementary or backup neural resources; the contrast with the finding is about how many neurons birds have.

sources.what: Vanderbilt University news on Olkowicz et al. 2016 (PNAS), senior author Suzana Herculano-Houzel with Pavel Nemec: parrots and crows match primates on complex tasks, raising the question of how birds with small brains manage it; birds have far more forebrain neurons than expected, smaller and more densely packed; the macaw has more forebrain neurons than the macaque; parrot and songbird brains hold about twice as many neurons as primate brains of the same mass

items.notes: Subject: natural science (neuroscience, ornithology). Key letter A. Lead author Seweryn Olkowicz credited (the press release names the senior author). Received view, then finding: the blank sits in the implied view and the finding’s trait (copious) is offered as the reversal, as in 3.10. Steps: 2 (small brains implied something about neural resources; the finding, introduced by But, is about neuron numbers, so the implication was scarcity). Near miss: specialized (the older idea that bird brains are wired differently) fails because the finding contradicts amount, not wiring. Raw freq.txt ranks: meager 20,689; copious 16,770 (reviewer: replaced ample 4,736, which sat a band below the other three); specialized 34,794; auxiliary 28,354.

fixes: distractor B ample (freq.txt rank 4,736, a band below the other three) replaced with copious (16,770); why_wrong B and notes updated

band7.why: Received view then finding, as 3.10: small brains implied scant resources and But overturns the amount. After the swap all four past 10,000 raw (16,770 to 34,794), 3 of 4 corrected (specialized 6,551), mean log10 4.18; key not the rarest. specialized is the near miss the finding does not contradict. Band-6 reasoning with no distractor past 50,000, so not band 7.

items.passage: Deadlines are often credited with motivating people to complete important assignments, but research by Meng Zhu, Yang Yang, and Christopher Hsee suggests that mere urgency can also make decisions less ______: participants often chose a task offering a smaller payoff over one offering a larger payoff because the former appeared about to expire.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Sagacious” means showing sound judgment. The text says that participants often picked a task with a smaller payoff over one with a larger payoff only because the smaller-payoff task seemed about to expire. Giving up the larger reward for no real reason is poor judgment, so urgency made their choices less sagacious.

A.why_wrong: “Improvident” means failing to provide for the future. Choices that were less improvident would be wiser, but the text describes participants giving up a larger payoff because a smaller one seemed about to expire, which is less wise, not more.

B.why_wrong: “Convivial” means friendly and sociable. The text is about how people choose between tasks with different payoffs, not about how sociable their choices are.

C.why_wrong: “Magnanimous” means generous toward others. The participants’ choices affected only their own payoffs, and the text says nothing about generosity.

sources.what: Zhu, Yang, and Hsee 2018, The mere urgency effect (Journal of Consumer Research 45(3)): across five experiments, participants chose tasks with objectively lower payoffs over higher-payoff tasks when the lower-payoff task merely appeared urgent (an illusion of expiration), violating dominance

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics). Key letter D. Band-7 moves: negation hidden in a comparative (less ______), as in d7807ec8; the key is an evaluation the reader must infer from the described choice (giving up a larger payoff for a spurious deadline); rare option set with the band-7 pattern of plainly unsupported rare distractors (band7 file section 2, point 4). All four options past 10,000 (15,764 to 29,905), mean log10 4.33, so checks 1 and 3 pass; check 2 fails (rarest distractor 29,905, under 50,000). improvident is a reversal trap for a reader who misses less. items.passage: Christopher Costello and colleagues found that fisheries managed with catch shares, which guarantee each holder a fixed portion of the total allowable catch, collapsed roughly half as frequently as others. By assuring fishers of their portion in advance, catch shares may ______ the scramble to harvest fish before competitors can.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “defuse” a situation is to make it less tense or dangerous. The text explains that catch shares guarantee each holder a fixed portion of the allowable catch in advance. A fisher whose portion is already assured has no need to race rivals for fish, so catch shares may take the pressure out of that scramble, which fits their link to fewer collapses.

A.why_wrong: To precipitate the scramble would be to bring it on suddenly. A guaranteed portion removes the reason to race rivals, so it would calm the scramble, not set it off, and the text links catch shares to fewer collapses.

B.why_wrong: To subsidize something is to pay part of its cost. The text says nothing about catch shares paying for fishing; it says they guarantee each holder a portion of the catch.

D.why_wrong: To ratify something is to give it formal approval, as when a government ratifies a treaty. The text does not suggest that catch shares approve the scramble; by assuring fishers of their portion in advance, they remove the reason to race rivals for fish.

sources.what: ScienceDaily (UCSB release) on Costello, Gaines and Lynham 2008, Science: catch shares guarantee each holder a fixed portion of a fishery’s total allowable catch; open access leads to a free-for-all race to fish and collapse; nearly a third of open-access fisheries have collapsed, about half that rate under catch shares; shares create an incentive to protect the stock

items.notes: Subject: social science (resource economics). Key letter C. Band-7 moves: the cause sits in a “By” clause in the blank’s sentence (recipe for B2); the key is a familiar word in a transferred sense (defuse a bomb, here a race), as in buttress or stymie; rare option set. Combined gate: 3 of 4 options past 10,000. Two-step chain: guaranteed portion, so no reason to race, so the race is calmed.

fixes: distractor D adjudicate replaced with ratify (44,154 raw, 17,822 corrected): read loosely, catch shares that assign portions in advance could be said to settle (adjudicate) the contest; why_wrong D and notes updated

band7.why: Cause in a By clause in the blank's sentence, like 0e033f9b (prudent) and a756aa95 (peripheral); key in a transferred sense (defuse a bomb, here a race). Options precipitate 14,384, ratify 44,154 raw (17,822 corrected), subsidize 74,107, defuse unseen in freq.txt (a corpus gap that inflates the mean log, 4.82); checks 1, 2 (subsidize) and 3 pass. All three distractors plainly fail on the text but are rare, the band-7 pattern in section 2, point 4.

items.passage: Comparing the scores of millions of students who completed a standardized test more than once, economist R. Jisung Park and colleagues determined that hot school days diminish students’ learning; that harm is not ______, however: in schools equipped with air conditioning, heat’s detrimental effect on learning largely disappeared.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Unavoidable” means impossible to prevent. The text says that hot school days reduce learning but that in schools with air conditioning, heat’s effect largely disappeared. Because air conditioning can prevent the harm, the harm is not unavoidable.

B.why_wrong: Park and colleagues measured the harm by comparing students’ test scores, so it is measurable; saying it is not measurable contradicts the text.

C.why_wrong: Saying the harm is not trivial would mean it is serious, which would not contrast with the finding that hot days diminish learning, as “however” requires; the evidence about air conditioning shows instead that the harm can be prevented.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how quickly the harm develops; the evidence about air conditioning concerns whether the harm can be prevented, not its pace.

sources.what: Park, Goodman, Hurwitz, and Smith 2020, Heat and Learning (American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 12(2)): student fixed effects models using 10 million students who retook the PSAT show that hotter school days before the test reduce scores; school air conditioning largely offsets the effect

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics of education). Key letter A. Lead author R. Jisung Park. The test is named only as a standardized test (the PSAT in the source). Negated frame (not ______, however) as in 2.21. Universal and lasting avoided as options: “not universal” would also fit (air-conditioned schools were spared) and “not lasting” could be misread with “disappeared”. Raw freq.txt ranks: unavoidable 16,320; measurable 32,842; trivial 6,377; gradual 9,216.

items.passage: The male gametes of the alga Gracilaria gracilis lack any means of propulsion, so researchers presumed that currents transported them to female plants. But Emma Lavaut and colleagues discovered that isopods, small crustaceans, act as ______ the alga, collecting gametes while foraging on male strands and transferring them to females.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A courier is someone who carries and delivers things. The text says the isopods collect the alga’s male gametes while foraging on male strands and transfer them to female plants, doing the carrying that researchers had assumed currents did. They therefore act as couriers for the alga.

A.why_wrong: The text does not say the isopods live off the alga at its expense; it says they carry its gametes to female plants, which helps the alga reproduce.

B.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that the isopods compete with the alga for anything; they carry its gametes from male to female plants.

C.why_wrong: The text describes the isopods foraging on the alga’s strands, so if anything the alga is the host and the isopods its visitors; nothing suggests the alga lives on or in the isopods.

sources.what: ScienceAlert on Lavaut et al. 2022, Science (Emma Lavaut, Sorbonne University): the red alga Gracilaria gracilis has male gametes with no flagellum to propel them; it was thought to rely on ocean currents; the isopod Idotea balthica inadvertently collects spermatia while foraging on male strands and transfers them to female plants; fertilization about 20 times higher with isopods present

items.passage: From the 1930s until 1943, the Works Progress Administration employed carriers, predominantly women, to deliver library materials to isolated households throughout mountainous eastern Kentucky. Because creek beds and animal trails frequently constituted the only roads, the carriers depended chiefly on horses and mules, animals capable of ______ terrain that automobiles could not.

items.passage:
The following text is from Charlotte M. Yonge’s 1853 novel The Heir of Redclyffe. Guy, a young man mourning his grandfather’s sudden death, is conversing with Mrs. Edmonstone.

‘Yes,’ he said; ‘how few Sundays ago—’ and there he paused.

‘Ah! you had so little preparation.’

‘None. That very morning he had done business with Markham, and had never been more clear and <u>collected</u>.’
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “collected” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: In the text, “collected” means calm. Guy explains that his grandfather’s death came without warning: that very morning his grandfather had handled business and had never seemed more clear-headed and composed.

B.why_wrong: “Collected” can mean fetched, as in collecting a child from school, but Guy is describing his grandfather’s state of mind that morning, not someone being picked up.

C.why_wrong: “Collected” can mean saved, as in collected stamps, but Guy is describing how his grandfather seemed, not something that was kept.

D.why_wrong: “Collected” can mean accumulated, as in dust collecting on a shelf, but Guy is describing his grandfather as clear-headed and composed, not something that piled up.

items.passage: In studies by Cassie Mogilner and colleagues, participants who spent time helping others subsequently felt less ______ time than participants who wasted time, spent it on themselves, or even received a windfall of free time. Giving time away, it seems, can make time feel more abundant.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: Someone “pressed for” time feels they do not have enough of it. The text says that giving time away can make time feel more plentiful, so the people who helped others felt less pressed for time than the people in the other groups.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how interested the participants were in time; it is about whether time felt plentiful.

B.why_wrong: The text does not discuss pride; it says that helping others made time feel more plentiful.

D.why_wrong: Feeling less sure of time does not match the text’s conclusion that giving time away made time feel more plentiful; the text is about having enough time, not certainty.

items.passage: Over 30 years of collecting cliff swallows killed by vehicles on Nebraska roads, Charles Brown and Mary Bomberger Brown observed such fatalities decline dramatically as the birds’ average wingspan decreased. Shorter wings may enable a swallow to take off more quickly and pivot away from approaching automobiles, helping it ______ traffic.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “dodge” something is to move quickly to avoid it. The text says shorter wings may let a swallow take off more quickly and pivot away from approaching automobiles, which would help it avoid being hit by traffic.

A.why_wrong: The text describes how shorter wings help a swallow get away from cars, not how a bird might make traffic slow down.

B.why_wrong: To trail traffic would be to follow it. The text says shorter wings help a swallow pivot away from approaching automobiles.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that swallows harm cars; it is about how the birds avoid being killed by them.

items.passage: During Philadelphia’s 1793 yellow fever epidemic, many Black residents volunteered as nurses for the sick. When publisher Mathew Carey later accused some of them of theft and of extorting wages, Absalom Jones and Richard Allen, leaders of the city’s Black community, published a pamphlet to ______ the volunteers against his charges.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “champion” people is to speak up for them and defend them. The text says Carey accused some of the volunteer nurses of theft and extortion, and that Jones and Allen responded with a pamphlet set against his charges, so the pamphlet was written to champion the volunteers.

A.why_wrong: Evacuation belongs to the epidemic setting, but the pamphlet came afterward, in answer to Carey’s charges; it was not a plan to move the volunteers out of the city.

C.why_wrong: Quarantine belongs to the epidemic setting, but the pamphlet answered Carey’s accusations against the volunteers; it was not a measure to isolate anyone from disease.

D.recipe: reversal (ANT), action of the wrong party
D.why_wrong: Condemning the volunteers is what Carey did when he accused them. Jones and Allen published their pamphlet against his charges, which means they took the volunteers’ side.

items.passage: The Indonesian mimic octopus, first described in 1998, is a remarkably ______ impersonator: it extends its arms to resemble the venomous spines of a lionfish, flattens its body to resemble a flatfish, and conceals itself in a hole, exposing only two arms, to resemble a sea snake.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Flexible” means able to change easily to suit different situations. The text gives three examples: the octopus extends its arms to resemble a lionfish’s spines, flattens its body to resemble a flatfish, and exposes only two arms to resemble a sea snake. Because it reshapes itself to imitate such different animals, it is a remarkably flexible impersonator.

B.why_wrong: A clumsy impersonator would imitate others poorly, but the text describes three distinct and specific imitations, each achieved by reshaping the octopus’s arms or body.

C.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests that the octopus hesitates to imitate other animals; the examples show the range of animals it imitates.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about whether the octopus is aware of what it is doing; the examples show how many different animals it can imitate.

items.passage: Most birds build some kind of nest for their eggs, whether an elaborate woven cup or a shallow depression in the ground. Common murres, however, ______ nest construction entirely: these seabirds breed on extremely narrow cliff ledges, where each egg rests directly on bare rock and is never left unattended.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: To “forgo” something is to do without it. The text contrasts most birds, which build some kind of nest, with common murres, whose eggs rest directly on bare rock on narrow cliff ledges. Murres therefore forgo nest construction entirely.

A.why_wrong: To relish nest construction would be to enjoy it, but the text says murre eggs rest directly on bare rock, which shows that murres build no nests at all.

C.why_wrong: Hastening nest construction would mean building nests sooner. The text says murre eggs rest directly on bare rock, so murres do not build nests at any time.

D.why_wrong: Supervising nest construction would mean overseeing it, but the text says murre eggs rest on bare rock, without nests, so there is no nest construction to oversee.
